'''''Solanum mauritianum''''' is a small [[tree]] or [[shrub]] native to [[South America]], including Northern [[Argentina]], Southern [[Brazil]], [[Paraguay]] and [[Uruguay]].<ref name=Olckersa>{{cite journal |last1=Olckersa |first1=T. |last2=Zimmermann |first2=H.G. |title=Biological control of silverleaf nightshade, ''Solanum elaegnifolium'', and bugweed, ''Solanum mauritianum'', (Solanaceae) in South Africa |journal=[[Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment]] |volume=37 |issue=1–3 |date=October 1991 |pages=137–155 |doi=10.1016/0167-8809(91)90143-L }}</ref> Its common names include '''earleaf nightshade'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SOMA3|taxon=Solanum mauritianum|accessdate=17 November 2015}}</ref> (or "ear-leaved nightshade"), '''woolly nightshade''', '''flannel weed''', '''bugweed''', '''tobacco weed''', '''tobacco bush''', '''wild tobacco''' and '''kerosene plant'''.

==Description==
[[File:Solanum mauritianum04.jpg|Flowers|left|thumb]]
[[File:Solanum mauritianum07.jpg|thumb|left|Yellow fruits]]
The woolly nightshade is a multi-branched shrub or small tree between 2 and 4 meters high (but can grow up to {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall in the right conditions). The plant has a strong odor and a life span of up to thirty years.

The simple, entire, [[Glossary of botanical terms#ovate|ovate]]-elliptical large leaves are up to 40 centimeters long, 30 centimeters wide and are grey-green in color. The tip of the leaf is pointed, the base is wedge-shaped. They sit on 3 to 9 centimeters long [[petiole (botany)|petioles]]. They are dense, tomentose with hairy yellowish, long-stemmed, star-shaped [[trichome]]s.

===Inflorescence===
The slightly scented inflorescences are [[cymes]] of purple single flowers with a yellow center and sit on 15 centimeter long [[inflorescence]] axes. The [[sepal]]s are fused into a 2 to 3 millimeter long [[Calyx (botany)|calyx]] tube with 1 to 2 millimeter long lobes. The [[crown (botany)|crown]] is star-shaped and measures between 1.5 and 2.5 centimeters. The five [[stamen]]s sit on 1 millimeter long filaments. The [[anthers]] are egg-shaped and 2 to 3.5 millimeters long. The plant can [[flower]] year round but fruiting occurs in late spring to early summer. 

After flowering, spherical yellow berries up to 2 cm in size with numerous, flattened seeds 1.5 to 2 millimeters long form.<ref>
Hanno Schäfer: Flora of the Azores . Margraf Verlag, Weikersheim, ISBN 3-8236-1368-5 , p. 166 (English).</ref>

==As invasive species==
[[File:Solanum mauritianum 7th Brigade Park Chermside L1100315.jpg|thumb|Naturalisation in Australia]]
Woolly nightshade has become a widespread invasive [[weed]] in the [[Azores Islands]], [[Cook Islands]], [[Fiji]], [[Hawai‘i]], [[Java]], [[New Caledonia]], [[Norfolk Island]], [[Madeira|Madeira Island]], [[Solomon Islands]], [[Tonga]], [[Réunion Island]], [[Mauritius]], [[Madagascar]], [[Australia]], [[New Zealand]], [[India]], [[Sri Lanka]],<ref>{{cite news |first=Lalith |last=Gunasekera |title=Invaders In Knuckles Mountain Range |newspaper=Sri Lanka Guardian |date=October 2011 |url=http://www.srilankaguardian.org/2011/10/invaders-in-knuckles-mountain-range.html}}</ref> [[Nepal]], [[Vietnam]], [[Philippines]], continental [[Portugal]], the [[United States|US]] states of California and Florida and several [[sub-Saharan Africa]]n countries.<ref>{{cite web |title=Solanum mauritianum Scop.; Delic. Fl. Insubr. 3: 16 (1788) |url=https://www.worldplants.de/world-plants-complete-list/complete-plant-list/?name=Solanum-mauritianum#plantUid-353876 |publisher=worldplants.de |access-date=16 August 2022}}</ref><ref name=Database>{{cite web |url=http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=209&fr=1&sts=&lang=EN |title=''Solanum Mauritianum'' Weed Profile |work=Global Invasive Species Database |access-date=2009-08-30 |archive-date=2016-03-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160326093052/http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=209&fr=1&sts=&lang=EN |url-status=dead }}</ref>

It arrived in [[New Zealand]] in 1880, and is now well established and [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] from [[Taupo]] northward. Because of its ability to affect human health and because of its aggressive and fast growing character it is illegal in all areas of New Zealand to sell, propagate, or distribute any part of the plant, under the [[National Pest Plant Accord]]. It is poisonous and handling the plants can cause irritation and [[nausea]]. The dust-like fine hairs from the plant can cause irritation to the throat, nose, eyes and skin.

This plant has also become naturalized in [[Australia]], particularly on the east coast and in desert ranges (South Australia). In Australia this plant is known colloquially as "'''tobacco bush weed'''", although Australia possesses many species of ''[[Nicotiana]]'', which are more correctly known as wild tobaccos.<ref>{{cite web| title=''NSW WeedWise Resource'' |work=The NSW Government Department of Primary Industries database on invasive plants |url=https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weeds/TobaccoBush}}</ref> It is tolerant of many [[soil]] types and quickly becomes established around [[plantation]]s, forest margins, scrub and open land.

In [[South Africa]], [[biological control]] is being used in an attempt to manage ''Solanum mauritianum''<ref name=Olckersa/> – the flowerbud weevil ''[[Anthonomus santacruzi]]'' is being used as a control agent.  ''S. mauritianum'' is a favoured food plant of the [[African olive pigeon]] (''Columba arquatrix''),<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gibbs |first1=David |last2=Barnes |first2=Eustace |last3=Cox |first3=John |year=2001 |title=Pigeons and Doves |publisher=A&C Black |isbn=1-873403-60-7}}</ref> the [[Cape bulbul]], the [[black-collared barbet]], the [[red-eyed dove]] and [[red-whiskered bulbul]].<ref>{{cite web |title=''Pycnonotus jocosus'' |work=Global Invasive Species Database |quote=''Pycnonotus jocosus'' (red-whiskered bulbul) is a bird native to Asia which has become invasive to several parts of the world. It has been found to damage crops, compete with native species and spread invasive plants. |url=http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=1230 |access-date=2013-09-08 |archive-date=2013-12-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131230234744/http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=1230 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In New Zealand biological control with [[woolly nightshade lace bug]] (''[[Gargaphia|Gargaphia decoris]]'') has been attempted since 2010.

==Toxicity==
[[File:Solanum mauritianum (49090544656).jpg|thumb|Large, mature tree]]
It is alleged that all parts of the ''Solanum mauritianum'' plant are [[poison]]ous to humans, especially the unripe berries,<ref name=Database/> and furthermore that human fatalities have resulted from the consumption of the berries, and cases of fatal poisoning in pigs and illness in cattle have been reported in Queensland.<ref name=Everist>{{cite book |last=Everist |first=S.L. |title=Poisonous Plants of Australia |publisher=Angus & Robertson |year=1981 |isbn=0-207-14228-9}}</ref> 

However, mountain possums appear to eat it without ill effect, and stripping of bark, leaves, and terminal shoots has destroyed pure stands of ''S.mauritianum''.  Watt & Brandwijk state that horses, domestic chickens and all birds eat the fruit with impunity, and further state that no records of poisoning in children exist, casting doubt on contrary published accounts.<ref>{{cite book |title=Medicinal and Poisonous Plants of Southern and Eastern Africa |first1=J.M. |last1=Watt |first2=M.G. |last2=Brandwijk |publisher=Livingstone |year=1962 |isbn=9780608142944 |edition=2nd |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2ZjwAAAAMAAJ}}</ref>

The main [[toxic]] compound is the [[alkaloid]], [[solasodine]], with the highest content in the unripe green [[Berry (botany)|berry]] (2–3.5% dry weight).<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Vieira |first=R.F. |title=Avaliação do teor de solasodina em frutos verdes de Solanum mauritianum Scop. sob dois solos no estado do Paraná, Brasil |degree=MS |year=1989 |location=Curitiba |publisher=Universidade Federal do Paraná}}</ref> [[Solauricine]], [[solauricidine]], and [[solasodamine]] have also been found in ''Solanum mauritianum''.<ref name=Everist/>

==Synonyms==
[[File:Solanum mauritianum plant NC1.jpg|thumb|Invading a riverside]]
The name ''Solanum mauritianum'' was applied by [[Francisco Manuel Blanco|Blanco]] to ''[[Solanum erianthum|S. erianthum]]'' and by [[Carl Ludwig Willdenow|Willdenow]] based on [[Albrecht Wilhelm Roth|Roth]] to ''[[Solanum sisymbriifolium|S. sisymbriifolium]]''.<ref name = ss2006>{{cite web |work=Solanaceae Source |date=August 2007 |url=http://www.nhm.ac.uk/research-curation/research/projects/solanaceaesource/taxonomy/description-detail.jsp?spnumber=3754 |title=''Solanum mauritianum'' }}</ref>

In addition, wooly nightshade has a number of [[synonym (botany)|synonym]]s:<ref name = ss2006/>
* ''Solanum auriculatum'' <small>Aiton</small>
:''S. auriculatum'' Mart. ex Dunal in DC. is  ''[[Solanum granuloso-leprosum|S. granuloso-leprosum]]''.
* ''Solanum carterianum'' <small>Rock</small>
* ''Solanum pulverulentum'' <small>Salisb. (''non'' L.: [[Solanum tomentosum|preoccupied]])</small>
:''S. pulverulentum'' Nutt. ex Seem. is ''[[Solanum puberulum|S. puberulum]]''. ''Solanum pulverulentum'' <small>Pers.</small> is ''[[Solanum cutervanum|S. cutervanum]]''.
* ''Solanum tabaccifolium'' <small>Vell.</small>
* ''Solanum verbascifolium'' var. ''typicum'' <small>Hassl.</small>
* ''Solanum verbascifolium'' var. ''auriculatum'' <small>(Aiton) Kuntze</small>
* ''Solanum verbascifolium'' var. ''auriculatum'' <small>Maiden (''non'' Aiton: preoccupied)</small>
:''S. verbascifolium'' <small>L.</small> is ''[[Solanum donianum|S. donianum]]''; ''S. verbascifolium'' <small>Banks ex Dunal in DC.</small> is the same as the undeterminable ''S. stenorchis''. Many other ''Solanum'' species (''[[Solanum conglobatum|S. conglobatum]]'', ''[[Solanum erianthum|S. erianthum]]'', ''S. granuloso-leprosum'', ''[[Solanum hazenii|S. hazenii]]'', ''[[Solanum riparium|S. riparium]]'', and ''[[Solanum stipulaceum|S. stipulaceum]]'' <small>Roem. & Schult.</small>) were once considered varieties of the ill-defined ''"S. verbascifolium"'' too.
